headlines.title: As AI grips world, the thrill of collecting vintage computers is growing
headlines.description: Software engineer Josh Dersch loves old computers. He spends countless hours tinkering in his garage, trying to coax decades-old machines back to life. He estimates he owns more than 200 vintage computers and devices in his Seattle home. “It’s always been fascinating to me to see the origins of things,” Dersch said. “It’s a fun challenge to debug and repair. You can understand the entire system from top to bottom.” Dersch is part of a growing community of vintage computer collectors who are preserving the classic machines that helped launch the digital revolution. While Silicon Valley has since moved on to shaping the future of artificial intelligence, these hardware enthusiasts are intent on saving the Atari, Commodore and IBM machines that are ancestors to today’s laptops, wearable devices and smartphones. Where others see junk, people like Dersch see artifacts of computer history that are worthy of attention and respect. They delight in hearing the beeps and chimes of their childhood and firing up a low-def game of “Pong” or “Space Invaders.” “The enthusiasm for the history of computers and all the stuff around it is growing,” said Erik Klein, president of the Vintage Computer Federation, which organizes an annual festival at the Computer History Museum in Mountain View in the heart of Silicon Valley. Vintage computer festivals bring collectors together This year more than 3,500 people attended the two-day Vintage Computer Festival in early August that celebrated the 50th anniversary of Apple, founded in 1976 in nearby Cupertino, Calif. It featured a panel with co-founders Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne reminiscing about the company’s early days as a scrappy startup led by the late Steve Jobs. More than a dozen such gatherings have since sprung up in cities across North America, South America and Europe. Growing interest is reflected in more demand for vintage computers in online marketplaces, Klein said. Rare, iconic computers like the Apple-1 — the company’s first product — can fetch hundreds of thousands of dollars. Collectors exhibited the computer systems that they have painstakingly restored to their original working condition, allowing attendees to play with the computers built long before the internet, social media and AI transformed the world. Restoring the ‘grandfather of the modern computer’ Dersch drove down from Seattle to showcase the pride of his collection: the Xerox Alto. He spent years restoring what’s considered “the grandfather of the modern computer,” which was developed at the pioneering Xerox Palo Alto Research Center in the 1970s. The Alto was one of the earliest computers to move beyond text on screen and use the mouse and graphical user interface — such as windows, icons and cursors — that became the industry standard. The model famously inspired Jobs and Bill Gates to incorporate the technologies in their early products. Dersch’s exhibit featured a fully functioning Xerox Alto workstation with its boxy vertical monitor, chunky keyboard and mouse, as well as pizza-sized spinning disks that store tiny amounts of data by modern standards. “It’s fun to share what I’ve done with people. It’s fun to share in what other people have done,” Dersch said. “Also, there’s a consignment area where I can buy more junk to take home with me, so that’s always fun.” Klein, a Silicon Valley software engineering manager, was a passionate collector until his hobby overwhelmed his home and family life. He had as many as 150 computer systems — complete with accessories, documents and packaging — crammed into his closets and garage. He said his beloved collection had become an “albatross” and he worried about burdening his family. So he started selling and giving away his machines until he only had a few favorites left at home. Similar events for collectors spread around the world Now Klein channels his passion for vintage computers into organizing festivals, repair workshops, swap meets and other events as president of the Vintage Computer Federation. “So it’s really about evangelizing that history and evangelizing this hobby of maintaining, collecting and enjoying this vintage technology,” Klein said. Sellam Ismail is thrilled to see the collector community develop and mature since he organized the first festival in 1997, drawing about 150 hobbyists to a venue east of San Francisco. He ran the events for a decade. He later co-founded the Vintage Computer Federation, which runs festivals in the US and Canada. He’s helped other groups launch similar festivals in Argentina, Germany and Switzerland. “The community grew up. More and more people started getting old computers, started collecting them,” said Ismail, who once had a massive collection he stored in a warehouse. “Next year is the 30th anniversary. And I expect this to continue and grow even bigger.”

headlines.title: El Cerrito Plaza BART station closed after person found dead
headlines.description: El Cerrito Plaza BART station is closed as police are responding to a medical emergency inside the station. According to BART, a deceased person was found on the concourse level. Officials said there are no initial indications of foul play, and the Contra Costa County Coroner’s Office has been called to the scene. BART trains are continuing to run, but El Cerrito Plaza station remains closed to passengers. AC Transit is providing bus service between El Cerrito del Norte and El Cerrito Plaza stations on routes 72 and 72M. Route 27 is also operating between Downtown Berkeley and El Cerrito Plaza. BART has not said when the station will reopen.

headlines.title: BART changes schedules to reduce delays, crowding
headlines.description: New BART schedule changes took effect Monday, bringing adjustments that could shorten wait times for riders across the system. The biggest changes are at the Daly City station, where BART has changed how trains use the station’s three platforms. BART spokesperson Chris Filippi said the station is essentially being converted into a single-platform operation, allowing riders to use one platform for all trains. “We’re turning this essentially into a single platform station, which means riders just go to one platform for all of the trains,” Filippi said. “It simplifies things and, more importantly, eases a bottleneck in the system.” BART officials said the changes will improve train spacing throughout the system, reducing the amount of time riders have to wait if they miss a train. Fillipi encouraged riders to check the BART app or website before traveling because train departure times have shifted by a few minutes. “We’re really advising our riders to go to our app or website and get the latest information,” he said. “They will see their train times will have changed by a couple minutes, so we want them to be prepared for that.” In addition to Daly City, riders transferring at MacArthur and Bay Fair stations will also see schedule changes and are encouraged to pay close attention to the updated train times.

headlines.title: Zuckerberg manifesto sketches out Meta's ambitions for world-changing AI technology
headlines.description: Meta Platforms CEO Mark Zuckerberg laid out a vision Monday of what he said artificial intelligence can do for the world, imagining a future where everyone has their own, all-knowing AI agent that strives to improve all aspects of their lives. Zuckerberg detailed his ambitions for the technology in a 6,500-word essay published online where he also outlined why he favors open-source AI technology, in which developers make key components accessible for anyone to examine, modify and build upon. In a document derided by critics as fantastical, Zuckerberg said his company is working toward an era where everyone will have the tools to create new businesses, receive Ph.D.-level tutoring and provide personalized lifestyle tips. His 8-year-old daughter, he wrote, can already code her ideas and quickly produce videos. “Everyone will soon have invention superpowers,” Zuckerberg wrote. Zuckerberg warned of risks if control of advanced AI is concentrated with a select few companies, institutions or governments. On Monday, Meta also announced the release a new open-source AI model, Muse Glimmer, which can run on a personal computer, and Zuckerberg said the company would also would provide a way for developers to access a more powerful AI model, Muse Spark 1.2. Meta makes AI models, like several other tech companies, and uses them to power platforms such as Instagram and Facebook. The Menlo Park, California, company also makes them available to developers who can create their own apps and features. Skeptics urge a slower pace of AI development Critics said Zuckerberg was not reckoning fully with the risks inherent in AI’s rapid development. Noting recent incidents where AI models, including Meta’s own, hacked other companies on at least three separate occasions, Anthony Aguirre, president and CEO of the AI safety nonprofit Future of Life Institute, asked “what on Earth makes Meta think they — or anyone — could control something exponentially smarter, faster, and more capable?” “Meta’s chosen path is ultimately one of human replacement and disempowerment, but there is an alternate, pro-human path — one that brings about individual flourishing and scientific breakthroughs with controllable AI tools. What’s urgently needed now is for governments to facilitate a pause on advanced AI development and steer us onto the pro-human path — before it’s too late,” Aguirre said. Meta chief says AI should be broadly distributed In his essay, Zuckerberg outlined why he thought open source is a better path for fair development of AI. He warned that if control of AI “superintelligence” is too concentrated, it will lead to less favorable outcomes for everyone else. The key, he wrote, is finding a balance that ensures advanced AI is “broadly distributed” to empower billions of people equitably. Meta has long been a proponent of open-sourcing its AI models, but has struggled to keep up with rivals such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google that have not taken the same approach. Zuckerberg made what could be a veiled reference to Meta’s rivals without naming specific companies. “Most other labs are focused on building AI for companies, governments, or other institutions, so if those labs lead, then the balance of power will favor larger institutions over individuals,” he wrote. Zuckerberg also included policy recommendations for keeping the U.S. ahead of rivals, including China. The United States and its allies need to speed up building energy capacity and infrastructure to stay competitive, he said. Zuckerberg called for authorities to reconsider their position on “ distillation,” which involves training a less capable model on the outputs of a stronger one. The Trump administration has vowed to crack down on Chinese AI companies using distillation to extract technical features from U.S. AI models. Anthropic earlier this year accused China’s DeepSeek of using distillation. “Some have tried to frame distillation as harmful, but I think it is important to protect the principle that you can learn from anything you can observe,” Zuckerberg said. “This is how the world works, and the U.S. will not be able to lead if we restrict ourselves on this front.” Critics see a self-serving message from Meta Matt Lane, senior policy counsel at the nonprofit digital rights advocacy group Fight for the Future, called Zuckerberg “annoyingly out of touch on his best day,” but said the CEO is right about the importance of open-source AI. Shared access to open-source AI systems is important for protection in a world where AI can be used to hack into electronic systems, like voting systems and benefits infrastructure, he said. But he said only Meta will benefit if everyone were to use Meta-designed AI systems, even if they are fully open-source. “Open source AI needs to be supported beyond these corporate interests. We, unlike Zuckerberg, hope for as much competition as possible,” he said.
headlines.source: Kelvin Chan | The Associated Press and Barbara Ortutay | The Associated Press

headlines.title: More evacuation orders issued for Timber Fire in Monterey County
headlines.description: More residents in the Loma Vista area of Big Sur, in Monterey County, were told to evacuate Monday afternoon as the Timber Fire burning to the east reached about 1,300 acres. Residents in evacuation zone MRY-F025–which is east of state Highway 1, from Mule Canyon Creek to south of Big Sur River Gorge–were told to evacuate immediately in orders from the Monterey County Sheriff’s Office at about 1:40 p.m. Zones MRY-F026, MRY-F027, and MRY-F028-A remained under evacuation orders Monday afternoon. A map of evacuation zones can be found at alertmry.org/alerts. Zones MRY-F024, MRY-F028, and MRT-F028-B were under warnings that could change at any time. Residents in the surrounding areas of state Highway 1 should be prepared to leave immediately if an order is given. A temporary evacuation point was established by the county’s Department of Emergency Management at the California State Parks Big Sur Station / Multi-Agency Facility, located at 47555 Highway 1. It was opened Monday and will be available from midnight to 7 p.m. each day through Thursday, or until evacuation orders are lifted, according to the county. Comfort kits including water and snacks will be provided by the American Red Cross. The temporary evacuation point serves as a location to get information and coordinate next steps, according to a statement from the county. Cal Fire activated an incident management team led by senior ranking fire specialists that will take command of the fire from the U.S. Forest Service at 4 p.m. Monday. The Timber Fire started Sunday afternoon and quickly grew to several hundred acres. It was 5% contained as of Cal Fire’s latest update Monday afternoon.

headlines.title: 2 cats die in fire caused by cigarettes in SF's Lower Nob Hill
headlines.description: Two cats died in an early Monday morning fire caused by discarded cigarettes in San Francisco’s Lower Nob Hill neighborhood, fire officials said. The fire was reported at 12:16 a.m. in the 900 block of Geary Street at a five-story, multi-residential complex. Crews had the fire contained and under control by 12:58 a.m., according to the San Francisco Fire Department. Fire officials said there were no persons reported injured and, as of 1:10 a.m., no residents were displaced. The fire was caused by discarded cigarettes in a single apartment unit, the department said. Firefighters remained at the scene to clear the area. The public is asked to avoid the scene while clearing operations are ongoing.

headlines.title: Man fatally shot in East Oakland
headlines.description: Oakland police are investigating a fatal shooting that occurred Saturday afternoon in East Oakland. Officers responded at about 3:30 p.m. to the 800 block of 75th Avenue after receiving a report of an unresponsive person in the street. When officers arrived, they found an adult man suffering from apparent gunshot wounds. Officers attempted life-saving measures before the victim was taken to a hospital, where he later died. The Oakland Police Department’s Homicide Section is investigating the circumstances surrounding the shooting. The victim’s identity is being withheld pending notification of next of kin. The investigation remains ongoing. Anyone with information, photos or video related to the case is asked to contact the Oakland Police Department’s Homicide Section at (510) 238-3821, the Tip Line at (510) 238-7950, or email cidvideos@oaklandca.gov. Police reference report No. 26-033930.

headlines.title: Former Warriors coach, Naismith Basketball Hall of Famer Don Nelson dead at 86
headlines.description: Some, giggling at some of his imaginative lineups, called him the mad scientist of the NBA. Others considered him cunning, even ruthless, a shrewd behind-the-scenes manipulator with a gift for obscuring his ulterior motives with a smile or a joke. Don Nelson was all that and more. The former Golden State Warriors coach who in 2012 entered the Naismith Memorial Hall of Fame, died Sunday at age 86. It is conceivable that no coach in NBA history did more moving and shaking and feuding, on the court and off, than Nelson. No coach did more winning, either, until one of Nelson’s disciples, San Antonio’s Gregg Popovich, supplanted him atop the NBA’s career wins list in March 2022. “Don Nelson was a true innovator whose influence on the game of basketball is still felt today,” Warriors coach Steve Kerr wrote in a statement. “He consistently challenged conventional thinking, experimented with different lineups and styles of play and saw possibilities in the game that others often did not. So much of what is now commonplace in the modern NBA can be traced back to the way Nellie approached the game. His impact on the Warriors is just as significant. He helped shape some of the most memorable teams and moments in franchise history and built a lasting connection with generations of Warriors fans. His legacy will always remain an important part of this organization. My thoughts are with the entire Nelson family.” “One of the big reasons I was drafted by the Warriors was because of Don Nelson,” Warriors superstar Steph Curry wrote. “The story is he never liked rookies, but from Day 1 he challenged me and gave me an opportunity to be my best self on the court. He taught me a lot during our one season together and I’ll never forget the night he became the winningest coach in NBA history in Minnesota. We were so happy for him. He had an immeasurable impact on the sport and will go down as one of the greatest minds in the history of the game. He’s a true icon and will be missed by the countless number of people he touched, including myself, during a legendary career. Sending my love to Joy, his family and all those who were fortunate enough to know him.” Nelson was the first coach to make copious use of a “point forward,” running plays through Marques Johnson and Paul Pressey in Milwaukee, though Rod Higgins and Chris Mullin and Stephen Jackson in Golden State. Nelson displayed considerable ingenuity with schemes that generated offense but never devoted much attention to defense. Which is how Nelson executed one of the great magic tricks in sports. He retired in 2010 with more wins than any coach the league had ever known yet never won a championship or reached The Finals. Nelson spent 31 seasons coaching four different NBA teams, serving two terms with the Warriors – 1988-94, 2007-10 – both of which mixed excitement before devolving into controversy or animosity. As Golden State coach/general manager in the late 1980s and early ‘90s, Nelson was the architect of the fabled Run-TMC teams featuring Hall of Famers Tim Hardaway, Mitch Richmond and Chris Mullin. After so many sub-mediocre seasons, the enthusiasm for those teams made Nelson a Bay Area celebrity so popular that he would receive standing ovations at the Oakland Coliseum Arena when walking onto the court before tipoff. Yet it was Nelson who, after coaching Run-TMC for two seasons, the second of which included a first-round playoff sweep of the Utah Jazz, dismantled the trio by trading Richmond. The move blew up the team’s strong chemistry. It took 16 years, with eight coaches cycling through the franchise, for the Warriors to win another postseason series; Nelson later acknowledged the trade was his biggest regret. Yes, even bigger than his mismanagement of Chris Webber. The first overall pick in the 1993 draft lasted one season, in which he was named Rookie of the Year. Nelson, headstrong, made few sincere attempts to connect with the big man of his dreams and their differences quickly became irreconcilable. The Warriors were swept by Phoenix in the first round of the 1994 playoffs. Webber was traded within six months, with Nelson resigning three months later. Eighteen months after Golden State was positioned to become a perennial playoff team, the franchise plummeted to its nadir, with Webber getting some of the blame but the brunt of it directed at Nelson. After one uneasy season coaching the New York Knicks, Nelson took a year off before being hired by the Dallas Mavericks. After three sub-.500 seasons, Nelson guided a roster featuring Steve Nash and young Dirk Nowitzki to four consecutive playoff berths, including his first conference finals. That run also ended bitterly, with Nelson and high-profile team owner Mark Cuban accusing each other of lies and deceit. Nelson filed a lawsuit than ended with him receiving a $6.3 million settlement through arbitration. By which time Nelson had returned to the Warriors – and taken them to the playoffs. Mullin, then the general manager, persuaded his former coach, then 66, to return to the sideline. Mullin then made a midseason trade to acquire Stephen Jackson and Al Harrington, who along with incumbent point guard Baron Davis, presenting Nelson with a satisfying roster that finished 42-40 and became the “We Believe” Warriors. Earning the No. 8 seed, they achieved one of the biggest upsets in playoff history, taking down the top-seeded Mavericks. It was a particularly tasty triumph for the coach. The euphoria lasted one season. Though the Warriors made significant improvement in the regular season, finishing 48-34, their efforts went for naught in an exceedingly rare season in which eight teams in the West won at least 50 games. A few months later, Nelson and Davis were at odds, with Mullin in the uncomfortable role of referee – while also trying to re-sign in the point guard. Golden State president Robert Rowell nixed the Davis deal, which led to friction among all involved parties. Nelson lasted two more seasons, both wretched. Through it all, Nelson retired as the most imaginative coach the Warriors had ever known. Moreover, he left them with a gift that serves as glorious restitution for his sins: Nelson selected a point guard named Stephen Curry in the first round of the 2009 draft. headlines.title: Timber Fire burns over 300 acres in Monterey County, prompts evacuation warning
headlines.description: A fire burning south of Loma Vista in Monterey County has prompted an evacuation warning Sunday, according to the Monterey County Sheriff’s Office. The sheriff’s office said it issued an evacuation warning related to the fire, named Timber Fire, for areas of Big Sur near Partington Ridge Road and North Coast Ridge Road, for the MRY-F026 and MRY-F027 zones. According to Cal Fire, the Timber Fire has already burned 400 acres and was 20% contained. The sheriff’s office added the evacuation warning excluded the Ventana Inn. The cause of the fire is unknown.

headlines.title: Phone ban at Oakland Unified goes into effect
headlines.description: Quite a few Bay Area school districts start their new year on Monday, including Oakland Unified, where schools have new cell phone restrictions. It’s part of a statewide mandate requiring districts to have policies limiting or banning the use of cell phones on campus. Some school districts across the state, including San Jose Unified, began implementing their own policies in 2025. Oakland Unified is one of the last major school districts to roll this out. OUSD alerted families that the new cell phone rules began on Monday when classes started. The district said that generally, elementary school kids will keep phones in locked classroom boxes. Middle and high school students will store cell phones in special Yondr pouches during the school day, which they can carry with them, but can’t unlock until the end of the school day. The district says phones also are allowed for documented medical needs and individual education plans. Staff can unlock phones that have been locked away if there’s an emergency as well. Some parents and students NBC Bay Area spoke with on Sunday were generally in favor of the policy. “Kids should not have phones at school, especially when they’re trying to learn,” said Charlie An, a parent of an OUSD elementary school student. “Phones, I think, just take their attention away from learning and being able to absorb critical information that they need form school,” he continued.

headlines.title: 2 pedestrians hurt after being struck by a pickup truck in San Francisco
headlines.description: Two people were taken to the hospital after being struck by a pickup truck in San Francisco on Sunday, according to the fire department. Authorities said a pickup truck hit two pedestrians and crashed into a light pole shortly before 12:30 p.m. on O’Farrell and Cyril Magnin streets. The pedestrians were taken to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, according to the fire department. They added two people in the truck were treated and released at the scene. The fire department said the police department is investigating the cause of the crash.

headlines.title: Festivals in San Francisco draw thousands of people to the city over the weekend
headlines.description: The Outside Lands Music Festival drew tens of thousands of people to Golden Gate Park over three days, but there were other events, including music at the Stern Grove Festival. In San Francisco, people lined up to see a performance at Stern Grove with an artist they’ve been waiting to see. For a fan, the choice of getting to the city from the East Bay did not involve driving. “I caught BART and Muni, but I actually had a smooth stop, I got off at St. Francisco circle and came off,” Tanna said. Sunday was the last day of this year’s Outside Lands Music Festival at Golden Gate Park. The festival was expected to draw a quarter of a million people over the three-day weekend, with a list of favorites. For Outside Lands, people could take special metro shuttles or the Judah Muni Line. Rideshare has drop-off spots and autonomous vehicles are restricted to rides a few blocks away from the park. SFMTA says it’s been going well getting people in and out efficiently. Across town, the annual Pistahan Parade and Festival returned to the city over the weekend. “This is the only Filipino festival here in San Francisco, so the community knows that this is the time for us to come together celebrate our roots uplift our community and enjoy some Filipino food and some entertainment,” Filipino American Arts Exposition President Al Perez said.
